content.title: Official Blind Review #3
content.review:
This paper explores the task of summary-to-article generation, the task of generating long articles given a short summary. Generating long text as output is challenging, since the seq2seq model often fall into degeneration of language models. To address this issue and have a better control on the long-form text generation, this paper proposes a hierarchical generation approach which first generates an intermediate sketch of the article and then generated the full article. This intermediate sketch can be noisy during inference because of the discrepancy between the training and inference strategies. To this end, this paper proposes a multi-agent reinforcement learning as well. 

For the evaluation of such long-form text outputs (article), this paper also proposes to use a summarization model to summarize the generated article and measure the ROUGE score between the generated summary and ground-truth. The premise here is that if we can generate a good article, then the output summary generated based on this article as input will also be good. 

They empirically evaluated the proposed hierarchical model with reinforcement learning, showing significant improvements over conventional seq2seq models. 

Overall, this paper is interesting with some new ideas, with caveat for some clarifications and missing some important experiments. 

Arguments:


1) It would be interesting to see how does a fine-tuned GPT-2 model on these summarization datasets perform on this article generation task. 

2) ROUGE-rec metric is weird in the sense that if the summary-to-article model just copies the summary with some junk non-related information which is fluent, the summarization model based on this article can still generate a good summary. However, this might not be the case as the human evaluation correlation is good with this metric. Anyway, I would suggest to further analyse this metric.

3) By seeing the outputs generated by the conventional seq2seq model, I was wondering if the repetition can be fixed by simply blocking the n-gram repeats. Further, I would be interesting  to see if transformers are better baselines in such long-form text generation tasks.

content.title: Response to Official Blind Review #3
content.comment:
Thanks for your valuable review and feedback!


Question: It would be interesting to see how does a fine-tuned GPT-2 model on these summarization datasets perform on this article generation task. 

Answer: It a good point. We will try it out in the future. However, as GPT-2 is a language mode and is trained to generate future tokens of the input summary, we think that the relevance of the generated article would not be good. This is also observed that the GPT-2 struggles to generate relevant sentences when the output becomes longer. Thanks for your valuable suggestion.



Question: ROUGE-rec metric is weird in the sense that if the summary-to-article model just copies the summary with some junk non-related information which is fluent, the summarization model based on this article can still generate a good summary.

Answer: ROUGE-rec measures the cycle-consistency The problem may exist but we find that none of our models learns to direct copy the summary. Actually, as ROUGE-rec is evaluated by a pretrained abstractive summarization model, which is sensitive to the input distribution. If the generated articles resemble real articles, it will produce good summaries about generated articles. If the generated articles are just summary + non-sense, then their distribution is far from training data of the employed summarization model and it may result in a low score. That is an intuition of the proposed ROUGE-rec metric. As it correlates well with human evaluation, we believe this metric is effective and may be valuable for future research in this domain.


Question:By seeing the outputs generated by the conventional seq2seq model, I was wondering if the repetition can be fixed by simply blocking the n-gram repeats. Further, I would be interesting  to see if transformers are better baselines in such long-form text generation tasks. 

Answer: Good point, we have tried that but it results in much shorter articles, which may because conventional seq2seq fails to extend the original input with a very large ratio. We have also tried transformers, but preliminary results show that the performance of the transformer is much worse than conv-seq2seq. We think that it may be because that the transformer architecture is not good at modeling long range dependency in the decoder, which is shown in the transformer-XL paper. Replacing the transformer with transformer-XL may be helpful, but is beyond the scope of this paper.

content.review:
This paper presents a new task on generating articles from their corresponding summaries. They propose a two-step generation process, where a sketch is first generated from the summary, and then the articles is generated from the sketch. Reinforcement learning is used for model training. 

I think the task is interesting. My major concern lies in the evaluation. Since the task is about article-level generation, i.e. long text generation, it would be necessary to evaluate the structure or discours flow of the text in addition to relevance. It is not extremely hard for neural models to generate content that is relevant to the prompt (e.g. summaries), from my opinion, the difficulty comes from how to maintain a coherent and connective discourse flow rather than drifting away to various topics or producing repetitive or generic content. However, none of these aspects is evaluated in the submission. I would suggest the authors consider these generation quality aspects. 


Other comments:
- The lengths of the generated articles should be reported, since different lengths of articles would significantly affect the perception of their relevance and quality.

- The author should commment on ethical concerns of the task. Since the summary only contains a subset of the information from the article, the model tends to generate fabricated content by filling in the rest of the narrative. This issue should be addressed in the discussion section. 

- Fig 8&9 captions are incorrect.

content.title: Response to Official Blind Review #1
content.comment:
Thanks for your valuable review and feedback!

Question: I would suggest the authors consider these generation quality aspects of the structure or discourse flow. 

Answer: We totally agree with your point. However, we find it difficult to evaluate this point and previous work only evaluates the perplexity of ground-truth text under the trained model as the quality of the generated long text. We find this to be troublesome and further evaluate the quality of generated articles by GPT-2. We think it may better reflect the coherence of the generated article. We would be grateful if you can suggest some metrics related to the discourse flow of generated articles. We also consider adding a human evaluation of the discourse flow of generated articles in the future version of our paper. Thanks for your suggestion!


Question: The lengths of the generated articles should be reported, since different lengths of articles would significantly affect the perception of their relevance and quality.

Answer: Thanks for your suggestion! We have included the lengths of the generated articles in our paper.


Question: The author should comment on ethical concerns of the task. Since the summary only contains a subset of the information from the article, the model tends to generate fabricated content by filling in the rest of the narrative. This issue should be addressed in the discussion section.  - Fig 8&9 captions are incorrect.

Answer:  We agree with your point and have included a discussion about this issue in the newest version. We have also fixed the captions of Fig 8&9. Thanks for your suggestion!

content.title: Official Blind Review #1
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I carefully checked the derivations and theory.
content.review:
This paper explores generating articles from summaries--- the inverse problem of document summarization. Since directly generating a long article from summary results in degenerations such as repetitions (appendix), here the authors proposed to generate a "sketch" of an intermediate length (the geometric mean of summary length and article length), then generate the article based on both the sketch and the summary. The sketch supervision comes from extracting sentences in the article close to the summary in the embedding space (using BERT), and both generation problems (summary -> sketch, summary+sketch -> article) can be trained with MLE. Then the whole pipeline is finetuned using policy gradients, where the reward signal for the sketch generator is the log likelihood of the article generator. In terms of modeling, the authors use a gating mechanism to combine summary and sketch states in the article decoder.

Experiments are conducted on two summarization datasets in the reverse direction (CNN/DM and BigPatent). To evaluate the generations' faithfulness, the authors proposed ROUGE-rec, which is based on another summarization system that summarizes the generated article, and use ROUGE-L as the score. To evaluate the generations' fluency, the authors used perplexity under GPT-2. The proposed method exhibits superior performance compared to normal seq2seq baselines, and human evaluations agree with ROUGE-rec and GPT-2 ppl.

Pros:
1. Most long document generation problems are open-ended such as pure language modeling. A closed-ended task like summary-to-article opens an interesting research venue.
2. The proposed model gets much better generations than the baselines, especially from the showed examples in the appendix.

Cons:
1. The proposed model has much more parameters than the baseline. It is not a fair comparison unless the baseline seq2seq gets the same number of parameters.
2. The proposed model relies on external models such as BERT for obtaining the sketches, which might give it an unfair advantage.
3. It seems that the baseline seq2seq models produce many repetitions even with nucleus sampling (appendix). I suspect they are not well trained.
4. With word/sentence perturbations, pretraining, and RL, there seem to be too many floating parts of the proposed approach.

Questions:
1. why does ROUGE correlate so poorly with pairing accuracy? (table 5)
2. what's the baseline reward R_t in Eq 2? Does that come from a neural network as well?
3. after pretraining, is Eq 2 the only objective for the sketch generator? Or do you need to mix it with MLE?

Minor：
1. table 6, human evaluation, column pairing accuracy, should make 68.3 bold instead of 65.0.
2. figure 2 is too small, hard to read

Overall, this work considers a very interesting problem, and by using a two-phase generation approach, this work gets decent performance in terms of summary-to-document generation. However, I think the approach is not very novel and I am inclined to reject this paper.

content.title: Response to Official Blind Review #1
content.comment:
Thanks for your valuable review and feedback!

Question: The proposed model has much more parameters than the baseline. It is not a fair comparison unless the baseline seq2seq gets the same number of parameters.

Answer: We understand your concern. Indeed, we have also experimented with a larger seq2seq model with more parameters, but they appear to fail to be well trained with limited data in our datasets. So we believe that the improvement yielded by our approach comes from the novel decomposition and hierarchical generation scheme.


Question: The proposed model relies on external models such as BERT for obtaining the sketches, which might give it an unfair advantage.

Answer: We agree that BERT is an external model. However, it is only used to select sketches. According to our preliminary experiments, the performance of our model will not degrade a lot (still much better than baselines) if we simply select sentences that have the most word-overlap with the summaries as the sketches.



Question: It seems that the baseline seq2seq models produce many repetitions even with nucleus sampling (appendix). I suspect they are not well trained.

Answer:  As mentioned in the introduction, training a seq2seq model to perform summary-to-article generation is hard due to the gap of information between input and output.  We have tuned the hyperparameters of seq2seq baselines carefully. In addition, the repetitions can be reduced if we do not enforce the output length to be longer than a predefined minimum length, but that would lead to very short articles that are also undesirable. 

Question: With word/sentence perturbations, pretraining, and RL, there seem to be too many floating parts of the proposed approach.
Answer:  We agree that the proposed approach is a little complicated. However, all of the proposed approaches improve the performance of our model and they together make our approach stronger. The denoising pretraining and RL are designed to mitigate the gap between training and inference, which is an important issue for hierarchical text generation, and previous two-stage generation models did not mitigate this problem.



Question: why does ROUGE correlate so poorly with pairing accuracy? (table 5)

Answer: We think this is because ROUGE and BLEU do not account for the one-to-many property of open-domain text generation. That’s to say, a generated article can be related to the summary but very different from the ground-truth article in terms of n-gram statistics.


Question: what's the baseline reward R_t in Eq 2? Does that come from a neural network as well?

Answer: Yes, this is a common practice in reinforcement learning.



Question: after pretraining, is Eq 2 the only objective for the sketch generator? Or do you need to mix it with MLE?

Answer: Eq 2 is the only objective used for after pretraining. 


Other Responses:  Thanks for pointing out these problems! We have fixed these issues in the uploaded revised version of our paper.  The novelty of our paper is indeed two-fold, the problem is novel, and we propose a novel decomposition scheme for hierarchical generation, together with residual-like model fusion and reinforcement learning to bridge the gap between training and inference of decomposed text generation models, which, to our knowledge, is the first approach to mitigate this discrepancy problem. Thanks for your consideration.

content.title: Acknowledgement to the reviewers
content.comment: We thank the reviewers for their valuable comments and suggestions. We will consider the reviews carefully to improve our work. In the meantime, we will withdraw the paper.
